428.title: Bhakti — the first use of the word in the Upanishads (6.23)
428.hook: the very last verse of the Shvetashvatara uses a word that will one day fill India's temples with song
428.carry: to one who has the highest devotion
428.tomorrow: Block A close · the seven Upanishads in one sit
428.howItsDone: Bhakti is lived across Hindu traditions through kirtan and bhajan singing, temple worship, repeating God's name, and honoring one's teacher, and many devotees treat love of God as the heart of practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the paradox. Smaller than small, greater than great, hidden in the heart and spread past the stars. Did you look from a tiny thing to the sky? Today, the Shvetashvatara's last word. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

On a festival night at a Hindu temple, the sound can reach the street before you reach the door: bells, drums, a crowd singing the same name over and over, someone in tears at the front. That whole world of love poured toward God has a name, bhakti, devotion. You met it in year one with Mirabai and the saints. But where does the word first show up in these old texts? You have to read to the very end of the Shvetashvatara, to its final verse, to find it.
screen: `BELLS, DRUMS, ONE NAME SUNG.` → `THE WORLD OF BHAKTI.` → `WHERE DOES THE WORD BEGIN?`

segments.voice: Verse 6.23, in paraphrase: for the great soul who has the highest devotion to God, and the same devotion to the teacher as to God, these things that have been taught shine out. They truly shine out for that great soul. The Sanskrit for highest devotion is para bhakti. The word bhakti comes from a root, bhaj, that means to share, to take part, to belong to. Some teachers draw on that root: devotion as belonging, a share in God, and not only a feeling. Scholars often point to this verse as the first time the word bhakti appears in the principal Upanishads in this sense, devotion to a personal God. And it's a striking place to find it. This Upanishad has spent six chapters on the wheel, the swan, the fire sticks, the posture, Rudra the one Lord, the self smaller than small. And its last verse doesn't add more knowledge. It names devotion: the teaching shines, the verse says, for the one who loves. Notice the teacher, too. Devotion to the guru as to God is part of the same verse, and many Hindu traditions honor the teacher this way. Not everyone reads it alike: Advaita teachers often treat devotion as what readies the mind for knowledge, while devotional schools treat it as the goal itself. Later in this course, the Bhagavad Gita will make this word a whole path.
screen: `PARA BHAKTI: THE HIGHEST DEVOTION.` · `BHAJ: TO SHARE, TO BELONG.` · `THE LAST VERSE IS ABOUT LOVE.` · then, large: `IT SHINES FOR THE ONE WHO LOVES.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone or something you love without needing anything back: a person, a teacher, a place, or, if you pray, God as you know God. Let that feeling sit in your chest. Don't push it bigger. Just notice what it does to the body, the shoulders, the breath, the face. Then notice whether anything you think about while that love is present looks any different. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion, from a root that means to share or to belong. Its first appearance in the principal Upanishads is in the Shvetashvatara's last verse.
Your line: to one who has the highest devotion. Today, do one ordinary task out of love for someone, and notice whether it feels different from doing it out of duty. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

429.title: Block A close · the seven Upanishads in one sit
429.hook: fourteen weeks, seven Upanishads, one sit to hold them all, and the three words that tie them together
429.tomorrow: "Now, yoga." Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind
429.howItsDone: Hindu traditions treat these Upanishads as the heart of the Vedanta: students chant and study them with a teacher, and the great sayings, such as tat tvam asi and prajnanam brahma, are taught as summaries of the whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shvetashvatara's last verse: the teaching shines to one who has the highest devotion. Did you do one thing out of love today? Now, the last day of the Upanishads. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

Ninety-seven days ago, you started with one syllable, om, chanted at a Vedic sacrifice. Since then: dogs chanting for breakfast, a boy telling the truth at a teacher's door, a woman who asked what water is woven on, a man whose head fell off for asking too much, two birds on a tree, a wheel, a swan, a pair of fire sticks. Seven books. Fourteen weeks. Today, before we leave, we'll walk through all seven in one sit, and find the line that runs through every one.

The Chandogya, the first we read. Uddalaka hands his son salt dissolved in water and says: taste it here, here, everywhere. That essence is the self of all. Tat tvam asi: you are that. The Brihadaranyaka. Yajnavalkya won't let anyone pin the self down. Not this, not this. And Maitreyi asks the question that matters: what would I do with wealth that can't make me immortal? The Taittiriya. Five sheaths, from food to breath to mind to understanding, and at the very center, bliss. The Aitareya. The self enters the body through the crown of the head, and near its end comes one great saying: consciousness is Brahman. The Prashna. Six students wait a year to ask their questions, and every answer comes back to breath and om. The Mundaka. Two kinds of knowledge, a bow and an arrow, two birds, and rivers losing their names in the sea. The Shvetashvatara. The wheel, the swan, the one Lord, and the highest devotion. Seven voices, centuries apart, with different schools reading them differently. Advaita teachers hear in them one reality without a second. Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita teachers hear a self that belongs to God and is never simply erased. All of them treasure the same verses. And the thread they all pull on is Uddalaka's: what you are looking for is not far away. Tat tvam asi.
screen: `CHANDOGYA: SALT IN THE WATER.` · `BRIHADARANYAKA: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `TAITTIRIYA, AITAREYA, PRASHNA.` · `MUNDAKA AND SHVETASHVATARA.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Sit in the posture you learned four days ago. Seven breaths, one for each book. Breath one: taste the salt everywhere. Two: not this, not this. Three: go inward, sheath by sheath, to joy. Four: consciousness is Brahman. Five: rest on the breath itself. Six: the river reaching the sea. Seven: devotion, in whatever form is yours. Then let the rest of the sit be quiet, with three words underneath it: you are that. The bell holds the time.
Block A close. Ninety-eight sessions in seven of the principal Upanishads, from om at the Chandogya's opening to bhakti in the Shvetashvatara's last verse.
Your line: tat tvam asi. You are that. Tomorrow a new text begins, the Yoga Sutras. Today, look at one person you pass and quietly think those three words. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

430.title: "Now, yoga." Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind (1.1–1.2)
430.hook: the most famous text on yoga opens with a single small word, and defines yoga in four more
430.tomorrow: then the seer rests in itself
430.howItsDone: Students of yoga in many Hindu lineages begin study of the Yoga Sutras by chanting 1.1 and 1.2, often with Vyasa's classic commentary, and treat 1.2 as the definition the whole text unfolds.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Upanishads with three words: tat tvam asi, you are that. Did you think them, once, looking at someone? Today a new block begins: the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. Day four hundred thirty.

A yoga studio: mats, mirrors, someone holding a long, shaking plank. The book behind the word looks nothing like that. The Yoga Sutras are short threads of Sanskrit, gathered under the name Patanjali, and only three of those threads deal with posture. The rest are about the mind. And the book opens with a word so small you could miss it. One word, and then a definition that commentators have been unpacking ever since.
screen: `MATS, MIRRORS, A SHAKING PLANK.` → `SHORT THREADS OF SANSKRIT.` → `THREE ABOUT POSTURE. THE REST: THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.1: atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha means now, and in old Sanskrit books it marks a beginning: here the real subject starts. There's a traditional verse that says two sounds came first from the creator's throat, om and atha, so both are lucky words to begin with. Some teachers also hear a quieter meaning: now, when you are ready, after everything else has been tried. The word anushasanam is interesting too. Commentators read its anu, after, as a teaching that comes after: handed down, not invented on the spot. Then sutra 1.2 gives the whole definition: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Chitta is the mind, the whole field of thinking and feeling. Vritti means a turning, a whirl, the way water turns in an eddy. Nirodha means stopping, or holding still. So yoga, in this book, isn't a shape you make with the body. It is the moment the mind's whirling settles. Notice how plain that is. No god is named yet, no stretch, no secret. Just the mind, its movements, and the possibility that they can quiet down. The rest of the first chapter is a manual for that. Yesterday's Upanishads spoke of what you are. Patanjali's book, from a different school with its own map, starts with a practical question: what is the mind doing, and how does it settle, starting now?
screen: `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING BEGINS.` · `ANUSHASANAM: HANDED DOWN.` · `CHITTA, VRITTI, NIRODHA.` · then, large: `YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, spine upright. For a few breaths, simply watch the turnings: a thought arrives, it swirls, it goes. Don't fight them. Then, each time you notice you've been carried off, say to yourself, silently, one word: now. Atha. Not as a scolding. As a fresh start. Now, and settle back on the breath. Now, and settle again. Every return is the first sutra, said again. The bell holds the time.
"Now. The first word of the Yoga Sutras, atha: the teaching begins here, and so does the practice, every time you come back.
Your line: atha. Now. Three times today, when you notice your mind whirling, say the word silently, and let it be a fresh start rather than a correction. Day four hundred thirty.

431.title: Then the seer rests in itself (1.3–1.4)
431.word: Then the seer rests in itself
431.hook: when the mind's whirling settles, what's left? Patanjali's answer is the one who was watching all along
431.howItsDone: In Patanjali's yoga, practitioners learn to witness the mind's movements rather than become them, and many Hindu teachers describe meditation as resting as the witness, sakshi, behind thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atha, now. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Did you use the word as a fresh start today? Now the obvious question: when the turnings go still, what's left? Day four hundred thirty-one.

You're at a movie, completely absorbed. You flinch at the jump scare. You tear up at the ending. For two hours you are the story. Then the lights come up, and there you are, in a sticky seat, popcorn on your shirt, and you realize: I was here the whole time. The story was on the screen. I was the one watching. Patanjali's next two sutras are about that moment when the lights come up.
screen: `TWO HOURS INSIDE THE STORY.` → `THE LIGHTS COME UP.` → `I WAS WATCHING ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.3: tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Then the seer rests in its own form. Tada, then: once the mind's turnings are stilled. Drashtri, the seer: in Patanjali's system, pure awareness, which he also calls purusha. Svarupa, its own form, its true nature. Avasthana, abiding, staying put. So when the whirling stops, nothing is lost. The seer is simply left as it always was. Then sutra 1.4 tells you what happens the rest of the time: otherwise, the seer seems to take on the form of the turnings. That's the movie. Anger rises in the mind, and awareness seems to become anger. A worry spins, and awareness seems to be the worry. The word seems matters. In this system, the seer never actually changes. It only looks that way, the way the moon looks broken on rippled water. Teachers often use that picture: still the ripples and the moon's reflection is whole again, though the moon itself was never in pieces. Here Patanjali leans on an older school, Samkhya, which separates two things: purusha, pure awareness, and prakriti, everything that changes, including the mind. The mind is not the seer. It's the screen. Vedanta schools describe the seer and the world in their own terms, and the Yoga Sutras keep their own. But on this point they meet: the one who sees is not the passing thoughts it sees.
screen: `TADA: THEN, WHEN THE TURNINGS STILL.` · `THE SEER RESTS IN ITS OWN FORM.` · `OTHERWISE, IT SEEMS TO BE THE TURNINGS.` · then, large: `THE MIND IS THE SCREEN.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Let thoughts come as they will. Each time one arrives, notice it the way you'd notice a scene on a screen: there's a plan. There's a memory. There's a worry. Then shift your attention, just slightly, back toward the one who is noticing. You don't have to find it or describe it. Just lean back into the seat, the way you do when the lights come up. The bell holds the time.
Then the seer rests in itself. Sutra 1.3: when the mind's turnings are stilled, pure awareness abides in its own true form.
screen: `THEN THE SEER RESTS IN ITSELF — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the seer. The next time a strong feeling grabs you today, add three words in your head: I see anger, I see worry, I see hurry, and notice who is doing the seeing. Day four hundred thirty-one.

432.title: The five turnings — right knowledge, error, imagination, sleep, memory (1.5–1.11)
432.hook: Patanjali sorts everything your mind does into five kinds, and two of them will surprise you
432.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five vrittis as a map for meditation, labeling movements of the mind so they can be noticed and released rather than followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the seer, the one who watches the movie and is never in it. Did you catch yourself saying I see worry instead of I am worried? Today, what exactly is on the screen. Day four hundred thirty-two.

Ten minutes of an ordinary mind might go like this. Read something and understand it. Misjudge someone's tone in a text. Rehearse a conversation that hasn't happened. Remember the call to an aunt that never got made. Nod off for a second. It can feel like a thousand different things. Patanjali says it's five. Every turning of the mind, he says, is one of five kinds. And sutra 1.5 adds a twist before he lists them: each kind can be painful or not painful.
screen: `TEN MINUTES OF A MIND.` → `A THOUSAND THINGS? NO: FIVE.` → `PAINFUL, OR NOT.`

segments.voice: Here is the list, sutras 1.6 to 1.11. One: pramana, right knowledge. It comes three ways: perception, inference, and reliable testimony, like trusting a good teacher or a scripture. Two: viparyaya, error. Knowing something wrongly, a picture that doesn't match the real form. The classic example is seeing a coiled rope in the dusk and taking it for a snake. Three: vikalpa, often translated imagination, or verbal delusion. This is knowledge that follows words with nothing real behind them. Indian logicians liked the example of a hare's horn: you can say it, you can almost picture it, and it isn't there. Some teachers say a lot of worry lives here. Four: nidra, sleep. Here's the first surprise. Patanjali counts dreamless sleep as a turning too, a turning that rests on absence. The commentator Vyasa notes that you wake up and say, I slept well, so something was registering. Five: smriti, memory, holding on to what you've already experienced. And here's the second surprise: right knowledge is on the list. Even true thoughts are turnings. Yoga, remember, is the stilling of all of them, not just the wrong ones. Why bother sorting? Teachers say a turning you can name tends to loosen its grip. That snake in the dark is just a rope. That argument in your head is just vikalpa, words without an object.
screen: `RIGHT KNOWLEDGE AND ERROR.` · `IMAGINATION: A HARE'S HORN.` · `SLEEP AND MEMORY.` · then, large: `EVEN TRUE THOUGHTS ARE TURNINGS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. For this sit, you're a gentle sorter. When a thought arises, give it one of five labels, silently. Knowing: I hear a car. Error: I thought that was a voice, it was the fridge. Imagining: a conversation that isn't happening. Sleep: that heavy, drifting fog. Memory: something from yesterday. Don't argue with any of them. Label, and let it pass, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The five turnings. Right knowledge, error, imagination, sleep and memory: Patanjali's five kinds of vritti, the movements yoga learns to still.
Your line: five. Count them on one hand today. When a thought grabs you, ask which finger it is: knowing, error, imagining, sleep or memory. Day four hundred thirty-two.

433.title: Practice and non-attachment (1.12–1.16)
433.hook: how do you still the turnings? Patanjali gives two tools, and they pull in opposite directions
433.howItsDone: Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages describe abhyasa and vairagya as the two wings of spiritual life, practiced through daily meditation or prayer kept up over years and a steady loosening of craving.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five. Knowing, error, imagining, sleep and memory, the five turnings of the mind. Which finger did your thoughts land on most? Today, the two ways to still them. Day four hundred thirty-three.

Learning to ride a bike takes two things at once. Keep pedaling, keep showing up, keep pushing. And stop gripping the handlebars so hard that every wobble becomes a crash. Effort and letting go. Too much of one and the bike never moves. Too much of the other and it tips over. Sutra 1.12 is only a few words long, and it says the turnings of the mind are stilled by a pair like that.
screen: `KEEP PEDALING.` → `LOOSEN THE GRIP.` → `EFFORT AND LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.12: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. They are stilled by practice and non-attachment. Abhyasa, practice, is defined in 1.13 as the effort to stay steady there, in that stillness. Then 1.14 adds the fine print. Practice becomes firmly rooted when it is done for a long time, without breaks, and with devotion, or real care. Long, unbroken, wholehearted. No shortcut is offered. Vairagya, non-attachment, is defined in 1.15. It's the mastery of someone who no longer thirsts for things, whether things seen, or things only heard about. That second category is interesting. The commentators take it to include rewards promised in scripture, even heaven. So non-attachment isn't only letting go of dessert. It's letting go of spiritual prizes too. And 1.16 names a higher non-attachment still: when, from knowing the seer, one no longer thirsts even for the three strands of nature themselves. Notice how the two tools balance. Practice is the gas. Non-attachment is easing off a brake you might not know you're pressing. Practice without letting go becomes grim and grabby. Letting go without practice becomes drift. Patanjali isn't the only one to pair them. In the Bhagavad Gita, when Arjuna complains that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, Krishna gives the same two words: by practice and by detachment it can be held.
screen: `ABHYASA: THE EFFORT TO STAY STEADY.` · `LONG, UNBROKEN, WHOLEHEARTED.` · `VAIRAGYA: NO MORE THIRST.` · then, large: `THE GITA PAIRS THEM TOO.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. For the first half of this sit, practice: keep returning to the breath, gently, every time you drift. That's abhyasa, showing up again. For the second half, add vairagya: keep returning, but let go of wanting the sit to go well. Let go of wanting calm, wanting insight, wanting the bell. Just return, and want nothing from returning. Notice the difference between the two halves. The bell holds the time.
Practice and non-attachment. Abhyasa and vairagya: the steady effort to return, and the letting go of thirst, the two wings of Patanjali's yoga.
Your line: abhyasa, vairagya. Pick one thing you're working at. Today, do your part fully, and then, once, let go of needing it to turn out a certain way. Day four hundred thirty-three.

434.title: Samadhi with seed (1.17–1.18)
434.hook: Patanjali's deepest absorption comes in two kinds: one that still rests on something, and one that rests on nothing
434.tomorrow: the born-free and the rest of us
434.howItsDone: Teachers of classical yoga describe samadhi in stages, first with an object of meditation and then beyond any object, and students usually work for years with a single support, such as the breath, a mantra or a divine form.

segments.voice: Yesterday: practice and non-attachment, abhyasa and vairagya, the gas and the loosened brake. Did you do your part and let go of the result once? Today closes a week that crossed from one book into another. Day four hundred thirty-four.

Imagine a camera zooming in. First a whole hillside. Then one tree. Then one leaf on the tree, so close you can see its veins. Then just the light falling on the leaf. Then, strangest of all, the camera turns around and looks at the one holding it. Each step is narrower and finer than the last. Patanjali describes the mind's absorption a bit like that zoom. And then, in the very next sutra, he describes what happens when there's nothing left in the frame at all.
screen: `THE HILLSIDE, THE TREE, THE LEAF.` → `JUST THE LIGHT.` → `THEN: NOTHING IN THE FRAME.`

segments.voice: Samadhi means absorption: the mind so gathered on something that the scattering stops. Sutra 1.17 describes the first kind, samprajnata, absorption with awareness of an object. It comes in four stages, from coarse to fine. Vitarka: absorbed in something gross, like a physical object. Vichara: absorbed in something subtle. Ananda: absorbed in joy. Asmita: absorbed in the bare sense of I am. Hillside, leaf, light, the one holding the camera. In every stage, there's still something the mind rests on. A support. Later in the chapter, Patanjali gives this kind its name: samadhi with seed, sabija. Then sutra 1.18 describes the other kind. It comes from practicing the letting go of every support, and what remains are only the faint traces, the samskaras, the impressions left in the mind. No object at all. With seed, without seed. The seed is the thing the mind still holds, and anything held can sprout again. Now look back at the week. Day one, bhakti, the highest devotion. Day two, the seven Upanishads closed with tat tvam asi. Day three, a new book opened with one word, atha, now. Day four, the seer rests in itself. Day five, the five turnings. Day six, practice and non-attachment. And today, with and without: the mind resting on something, and the mind resting on nothing.
screen: `SAMADHI: THE MIND GATHERED.` · `FOUR STAGES, COARSE TO FINE.` · `1.18: NO SUPPORT LEFT.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `WITH SEED, WITHOUT SEED.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Let's do the zoom, gently. First rest your attention on something coarse: the whole body sitting. Then something finer: just the breath at the nostrils. Then finer still: any ease or pleasantness that's there. Then the simplest thing of all: the plain feeling of being here, I am. Stay there. If even that thins out for a moment, let it. Don't chase it, and don't try to hold it. The bell holds the time.
Samadhi with seed. Absorption that still rests on a support, coarse or subtle, joy or the bare sense of I am, as opposed to absorption with no seed at all.
Your line: with, without. Today, notice one moment you're absorbed in something, a task, a song, a conversation, and ask: what is my mind resting on right now? Day four hundred thirty-four.

screen: `DAY 434 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK FROM BHAKTI TO SAMADHI, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: THE BORN-FREE AND THE REST OF US.`
